title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in Vienna: Scale Route Maps ⚡
description: Watch Bidirectional Dijkstra expand from start and goal at the same time, meeting in the middle to cut search work. This visualization shows how modern route planning engines get “shortest path at scale” without brute-force expansion.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale ⚡—Ever wondered why some route searches feel instant?

In this Vienna (Innere Stadt) grid, the algorithm runs two Dijkstras simultaneously:
1) Forward search from the start node.
2) Backward search from the goal node.

Instead of exploring the whole map, each side expands the “cheapest-so-far” frontier until the searches meet. The moment the frontiers connect, you can reconstruct the shortest path using the best combined distance—often with dramatically fewer visited nodes.

What to notice in the animation:
• Two expanding waves (one from start, one from goal)
• Fewer overall expansions vs. classic Dijkstra
• The “meeting point” is the key to scaling

Takeaway: Bidirectional search leverages problem symmetry to reduce work—big win for route planning engines under tight latency budgets.

Debate question: Should bidirectional search always be your default shortest-path strategy, or does it break down when graphs are highly asymmetric?
